claims.statement: TanStack's postmortem says 84 malicious versions of 42 @tanstack/* npm packages were published on May 11, 2026 between 19:20 and 19:26 UTC, after a cache-poisoning step that began with a renamed fork of TanStack/router created the day before.

Researchers describe the May 11-12 wave as one self-propagating worm that reached about 170 npm and PyPI packages, including Mistral AI, Guardrails AI and UiPath packages, and say TeamPCP published the worm's source code on May 12, 2026.
Unit 42 says later 2026 waves, including June activity, reused the Mini Shai-Hulud code that TeamPCP open-sourced, which makes attribution of copycat waves harder.

unresolvedQuestions: Package counts differ by researcher and date (about 170 vs 400+); record each figure with its source.
Attribution to TeamPCP comes from researchers and the group's own claims, not from TanStack.
Whether to keep later copycat waves (May 19 mistralai PyPI takeover, June 'Megalodon') as separate records.

claims.statement: Grafana Labs says a cybercrime group gained access to its GitHub repositories, downloaded its codebase and demanded a ransom, which it confirmed on May 16, 2026 and chose not to pay.

Grafana Labs says the incident started with the TanStack npm attack on May 11, when malicious code ran on its self-hosted CI runners and leaked credentials; it rotated tokens, but one GitHub workflow token was missed and was later used to commit and exfiltrate repositories from May 14.

Grafana Labs says the impact was limited to its GitHub environment, including internal operational repositories holding some business contact names and emails, with no access to customer production systems or Grafana Cloud.

unresolvedQuestions: The bot account named in Grafana's timeline is a leaked automation identity; confirm the exact token type before tagging a secret type.
Mandiant's audit was announced; its findings are not public.

claims.statement: Mistral's advisory MAI-2026-002 says compromised npm SDK packages were live from May 11 to May 12, 2026 and a compromised PyPI release was live for about three hours on May 12, and that an affected developer device was involved with no impact on Mistral's global infrastructure.
TeamPCP claimed on a cybercrime forum to hold about 5 GB across roughly 450 Mistral internal repositories and offered them for sale; Mistral's advisory does not confirm repository theft.

unresolvedQuestions: Repository-theft claim is the attacker's; Mistral's advisory confirms only the SDK compromise.
A later September 2026 forum listing claimed a fresh Mistral breach, which Mistral denied; not included here.

candidates.dedupeCheck: No seed incident or candidate covers this. Reported as part of the same TeamPCP activity; the VS Code extension vector differs from the npm worm, so keep as its own record. Primary sources (GitHub's blog and the Nx Console advisory) added 2026-11-22.

claims.statement: GitHub's CISO wrote on May 20, 2026 that on May 18 GitHub detected and contained a compromise of an employee device involving a poisoned third-party VS Code extension, removed the malicious version, isolated the device and rotated critical secrets over the next day.

GitHub said the activity involved exfiltration of GitHub-internal repositories only, that the attacker's claim of about 3,800 repositories was directionally consistent with its investigation, and that it had no evidence of impact to customer data outside those repositories, though some internal repositories hold customer support excerpts.

GitHub's May 26 update says it is rotating keys as a precaution, including the GitHub Enterprise Server binary signing key, and GHES administrators must rotate the GPG public key on their instances before installing future updates.

The extension GitHub links to is Nx Console: its maintainers' advisory GHSA-c9j4-9m59-847w (published May 18, 2026) says version 18.95.0 was compromised, fetched an obfuscated payload that harvested credentials from disk and memory, and was fixed in 18.100.0.
TeamPCP claimed the theft and offered the data for sale.

unresolvedQuestions: GitHub promised a fuller report when the investigation completes; none was found as of 2026-11-22.
Customer impact from the support excerpts in internal repositories is not confirmed either way.
Attribution to TeamPCP rests on the group's claim and researchers, not on GitHub's post.

claims.statement: Singapore's Cyber Security Agency issued advisory AD-2026-009 on August 6, 2026 about malicious Keyv and related npm packages carrying a self-propagating Shai-Hulud-family stealer called ChainDrop, and advised treating credentials on affected systems as compromised.
Aikido says attackers took over the GitHub account of the keyv maintainer on August 4, 2026; its count reached at least 868 packages across 1,381 versions that day.
Elastic says the worm used stolen npm credentials to backdoor co-owned packages and created public GitHub repositories described as 'Shai-Hulud: Here We Go Again'.

GitGuardian says the first infected release was keyv 6.0.0 at 09:35 UTC on August 4 and the last known malicious package was published at 00:27 UTC on August 5, and that the payload belongs to the Mini Shai-Hulud family whose code was open-sourced in May.

unresolvedQuestions: Counts vary by researcher and time (about 420 to 868 packages); keep each figure with its source.
Attribution: some researchers tie this to TeamPCP, others only to the open-sourced code; do not attribute without a primary claim.
